newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ central bank sanctions fall in rates, dollar.
newsitem.headline: NZ central bank sanctions fall in rates, dollar.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand on Thursday sanctioned a fall in the New Zealand dollar and interest rates, but analysts said it was not a long-promised major easing of monetary conditions.

RBNZ Financial Markets Chief Manager David Archer sent 90-day bank bill rates tumbling and the New Zealand dollar spiralling down three quarters of a U.S. cent when he said a recent firming of conditions was greater than necessary.
Last week, the bank warned markets after a positive inflation number that conditions were easing too quickly. That caused the dollar to soar while interest rates only fell mildly.

However, in Thursday's statement, the bank appeared to recognise that its desire for a slightly lower currency and firmer interest rates in the monetary mix could not be achieved, and the rising currency was putting undue pressue on exporters.

"Unfortunately, in order to keep overall monetary conditions consistent with maintaining price stability, it appears that we will have to accept rather less interest rate pressure than might be ideal, and rather more exchange rate pressure than might be ideal," Archer said.

"They are admitting what we have known all along -- that they are caught between a rock and a hard place, that they are not going to get their preferred mix of monetary conditions," said Westpac Bank economist Joselyn Stroombergen.
She rejected any suggestion that the bank was signalling a major easing or that it was bowing to political pressure.
Leaders of both the Labour and New Zealand First parties have recently called for a lower dollar to help exporters.

An inconclusive general election was held on October 12 leaving nationalist New Zealand First with the balance of power between the left-of-centre Labour and the conservative National Party, which remains as caretaker government. NZ First is holding talks with both parties.

ANZ Bank treasury economist David Drage agreed the RBNZ was not signalling a major easing or bowing to pressure but was recognising exporters were suffering pain, with the Kiwi rising more than two U.S. cents since the election.
"To some extent the Reserve Bank is recognising the extra pressure the higher Kiwi has put on the tradeable goods sector.

"It's really the Reserve Bank prompting the market to adjust monetary conditions given the rise of the Kiwi over the past week," Drage said. "If monetary conditions ease too far on the back of this statement we'd expect the Reserve Bank to come out and indicate when enough is enough."
He expected 90-day bank bills to fall to around 9.0 percent. They fell to 9.05 percent from 9.30 percent before the statement.
Bond dealers said lower wholesale rates may feed into lower mortgage rates and possibly higher house prices, something Archer identified in his statement as a concern to the RBNZ.

However, Drage said that despite concerns about house prices, which have been largely responsible for sending inflation this year outside the RBNZ's 0-2 percent target band, there was a danger inflation late next year would fall below the bottom of the band if the Kiwi was allowed to run on unchecked.
